summary: Describes a strategy for resisting the Million Message Attack on the Cryptographic Message Syntax, where an attacker sends many chosen messages to learn a private key. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: The Million Message Attack uses a receiver's different reactions to test guesses about decrypted data. RFC 3218 describes ways for CMS implementations to hide those differences.

questions: how to prevent million message attack on cms
what is the million message attack
how does random filling prevent a padding oracle
subtitle: How uniform failure handling can prevent a padding oracle in CMS decryption.

tldr.problem: An attacker may recover an RSA-encrypted block by sending altered ciphertexts and distinguishing whether the decrypted block has valid PKCS-1 formatting.
tldr.mechanism: The memo recommends making different failure cases indistinguishable, most simply by replacing a malformed encrypted content key with a random key and continuing. OAEP is another padding method that is not susceptible to this attack.
tldr.outcome: Uniform behavior removes the signal the attacker needs. OAEP offers an upgrade path but is incompatible with existing PKCS-1 implementations described by the memo.

today: RFC 3218 is Informational. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Million Message Attack
sections.content:
RSA encryption uses padding to fill a block to the length of the modulus. Bleichenbacher described an adaptive chosen-ciphertext attack that can recover a PKCS-1 encrypted block if the receiver acts as an oracle.

In CMS, automated mail-list agents are a possible target because they process many messages. The attacker changes a captured ciphertext and uses the receiver's responses to learn information about the original plaintext.
sections.plainLanguage: An attacker sends changed versions of an encrypted message and watches how the receiver reacts. Those reactions can reveal information the private key is supposed to protect.

sections.title: The PKCS-1 Encryption Block
sections.content:
For encryption, a PKCS-1 block begins with a zero byte and block-type byte 2, followed by non-zero random padding, a zero separator and the message. The padding must contain at least 8 bytes.

CMS encrypts a symmetric content-encryption key (CEK) in this block. The receiver must recognize whether the block has the required format, which creates a risk if its response reveals the result of that check.
sections.plainLanguage: The encrypted key is surrounded by a defined pattern and random bytes. If the receiver reveals whether that pattern was valid, an attacker can use the answer as a clue.

sections.title: How the Attack Learns from Responses
sections.content:
The attacker transforms a captured ciphertext and asks the victim to process each result. Most decrypted blocks are malformed, but some have the expected first bytes and look properly formatted. The attack usually requires about 2^20 messages and responses.

The attacker must distinguish malformed padding from other failures, such as a wrong-length key or failed integrity check. Different error messages or timing can provide that distinction. The memo says a uniform response to all relevant failures prevents the attack.
sections.plainLanguage: The attacker needs the receiver to react differently when a guess is close. If every failure looks and takes the same amount of time, those reactions stop providing clues.

sections.title: Countermeasures
sections.content:
Careful checks of padding, CEK length and parity bits can make the attack require more probes, especially when the receiver responds identically to all such errors. Random filling is the simplest countermeasure: for malformed padding, substitute a cryptographically random CEK of the appropriate length and continue processing.

A fixed substitute key is unsafe because an attacker could create a message that decrypts successfully with it. OAEP is not susceptible to the Million Message Attack, but the memo notes that it is incompatible with PKCS-1 and therefore was not yet suitable for all widely deployed CMS implementations.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not tell the sender whether the padding was wrong. Use a fresh random substitute key and continue so the later failure does not reveal what happened earlier.
